title: Show Me How You Got Here:
author: Jen Shew
source: Leadership at the Edge of Change (jenshew.substack.com), August 26, 2026
summary: Jen Shew argues that AI has broken the traditional academic-integrity assumption that a polished final product reveals whether learning happened, and proposes replacing "prove you didn't use AI" with the question "show me how you got here." She illustrates the spectrum of AI use with four students writing the same essay, from AI-assisted brainstorming to full AI-generated submission, arguing that the diagnostic question isn't whether AI was used but whether it helped the student think more deeply or replaced the thinking they were supposed to be learning to do. Her practical mechanism is a short "AI Use Statement" students submit alongside assignments, paired with a traffic-light system (red for independent work, yellow for AI as a learning partner, green for AI collaboration as the learning objective) that sets expectations before the assignment rather than policing after. She closes by warning that if disclosure automatically triggers suspicion, students have no incentive to be honest, so building a culture where transparency is safer than hiding is the real work, one she is implementing across both a university (Lipscomb) and a K-12 school (Summit Christian School) with grade-band-appropriate scaffolding.
points: Replaces the academic-integrity question 'did you use AI?' with 'show me how you got here,' arguing the diagnostic that matters is whether AI helped the student think more deeply or replaced their required thinking.
Illustrates AI use as a spectrum with four students writing identical essays, from AI-assisted brainstorming with independent execution to a fully AI-generated submission with minimal changes.

Introduces a practical 'AI Use Statement' template (what I used AI for, what I contributed, one suggestion I rejected, what I learned) paired with a red/yellow/green traffic-light framework for setting assignment-level expectations.

Warns that if disclosing AI use automatically triggers suspicion, students have no incentive toward transparency, so building a culture where honesty is safer than hiding is the real institutional work.
quotes: In the age of AI, a polished final product no longer tells us enough about what learning has led the student to the piece they are turning in. What if we started with a different question: Can you show me how you got here?
All four students used AI, but they engaged in different intellectual processes. That's why simply asking, Did you use AI, is becoming less useful, especially as the tools evolve.

What we should be asking about AI use, then, just like we would with any other assistance, is, did the tool help the student think more deeply, or did it do the thinking the student was supposed to be learning to do?

We suggested a simple traffic-light framework for communicating expectations: red for independent work, yellow for AI as a learning partner, and green for assignments where AI collaboration is part of the learning objective.

If admitting that you used AI automatically places you under suspicion, then a student doesn't have any incentive to be transparent. Students learn cultures quickly, and if the culture communicates that the safest answer is I didn't use AI, then we shouldn't be surprised when students hide how they are actually working.
